name: Isaac Newton
major_ideas: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics
The removal of animism and purpose from physics
The relativity of motion and the abandonment of absolute space and time
biography: Russell traces the atomists' implicit commitment to absolute space forward to Newton's theory of absolute space, distinguishing absolute from relative motion, as the 'logical development' of the atomist view. Presented as achieving 'the final and complete triumph' anticipated by his three predecessors, deriving Kepler's laws from his own laws of motion and the inverse-square law of universal gravitation, and thereby unifying terrestrial and celestial mechanics; Russell notes the danger that Newton's authority, like Aristotle's before him, threatened to become 'an insuperable barrier to progress' for a century after his death.
central_doctrines: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics: Newton's law: 'Every body attracts every other with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them,' derived by showing that Kepler's three laws are equivalent to the claim that every planet has, at every moment, an acceleration toward the sun that varies inversely as the square of the distance. The removal of animism and purpose from physics: Russell's account: 'Lifeless matter, once set moving, will continue to move for ever unless stopped by some external cause... The solar system... was kept going by its own momentum and its own laws; no outside interference was needed.' God might still be needed to set the mechanism working initially, but 'when He had done this... everything went on by itself without further need of divine intervention,' and even the necessity of an initial Creator became doubtful once Laplace suggested the planets might have formed naturally from the sun.
key_arguments: From Kepler's three laws to Newton's law of universal gravitation

disagreements.about: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics
The removal of animism and purpose from physics

russell_view: Russell presents the rise of science as the true dividing line of modernity, crediting Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and Newton (in ascending order of achievement, with Galileo and Newton as the two greatest) with combining, for the first time together in a sustained way, patient empirical observation and bold, revisable hypothesis-making. He defends the scientific attitude explicitly against E. A. Burtt's charge that early modern science's success was merely lucky, arguing that what matters is method (tentative, evidence-based belief) rather than the immediate provability of any particular early theory. He is admiring but not uncritical: he notes Copernicus's residual Pythagorean aesthetic bias, Kepler's quasi-mystical motivations, and the danger that Newton's overwhelming authority threatened, like Aristotle's before him, to freeze rather than advance further inquiry. He closes the chapter by drawing out the era's deepest philosophical consequences -- the removal of animism and purpose from physical explanation, the destabilizing effect on orthodox theology, and the paradoxical way in which a cosmologically humbling discovery (earth's insignificance) produced not humility but a new, scientifically-fueled human self-confidence.
why_this_matters: Russell identifies the seventeenth century, not the Italian Renaissance or the Reformation, as the true beginning of the modern mental outlook, because of the transformative achievement of Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and Newton. Galileo's law of inertia (and Newton's codification of it as the first law of motion) unified terrestrial and celestial dynamics under a single principle: uniform motion is 'natural' unless changed by an external force.
